issues.legal_issue: A bona fide partition by all co-lessors can sever a tenanted property into identifiable portions, allowing the owner of an allotted portion to seek eviction from that portion.
material_facts: The shop had been jointly inherited by the landlord and his brothers and was let to the tenant while one brother managed it on behalf of the family.
The brothers partitioned the shop, and a defined portion fell to the landlord.
The landlord sought eviction from the portion allotted to him; the tenant had been informed of the partition.
The courts below had upheld the eviction order, but the High Court set it aside on the ground that the tenancy was indivisible.
The Court found no basis to treat the partition as a sham, while recognizing that a tenant may show a partition was not bona fide.
issues.conclusion: A bona fide partition among the co-lessors gives each owner separate rights over the portion allotted to that owner, including the right to seek eviction of the tenant from that portion. The tenant cannot prevent the partition, though the tenant may challenge it as a sham or device to evade rent-control protections.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 8, 36, 37 and 109 of the Transfer of Property Act, rights and benefits relating to property may be apportioned or pass with the relevant interest, and a tenancy is not perpetually indivisible. Section 109 applies its underlying principles to a severance by partition even if a family partition is not a transfer within Section 5. A co-owner cannot unilaterally split the tenancy, but co-owners who agree to a bona fide partition into definite, identifiable portions may deal independently with their respective portions and the tenant occupying them. The Court relied on Raja Simhadri v. PrattiPatti Ramayya, Sm. Durgarani Devi v. Mohiuddin, the authorities approved in Mohar Singh v. Devi Charan, and the principles concerning family arrangements and partition in Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, Ram Charan Das v. Giria Nandini Devi, V.N. Sarin v. Ajit Kumar Poplai and Giria Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiral.

rule.if: tenancy_eviction_proceeding and all_co_lessors_agreed_to_partition and partition_created_identifiable_portions and partition_was_bona_fide

predicates.tenancy_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant from leased property.
predicates.all_co_lessors_agreed_to_partition: All co-lessors agreed to divide the leased property among themselves.
predicates.partition_created_identifiable_portions: The division gave the owners definite, identifiable portions of the property.
predicates.partition_was_bona_fide: The division was genuine and was not a sham devised to evade tenant-protection rules.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding concerns a genuine division agreed to by all co-lessors that creates identifiable portions, the owner allotted a portion may seek eviction from that portion.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant must have notice or knowledge of a severance or transfer before becoming liable to pay rent separately to the new owner, but notice does not postpone the passing of title.
material_facts: After the partition, the landlord and the brother managing the property informed the tenant that the defined portion had fallen to the landlord and asked the tenant to pay rent to him.
The landlord later terminated the tenancy by notice after the tenant did not pay rent to him.
The Court treated notice of the severance as relevant to the tenant’s obligation to pay rent to the separate owner, while distinguishing that obligation from the passing of title.
issues.conclusion: Notice or knowledge of the transfer or severance is a condition precedent to making the tenant liable to pay rent to the transferee, but title passes when the transfer or assignment takes effect and is not postponed until notice is received.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 37 and 109 of the Transfer of Property Act require reasonable notice or knowledge before a tenant can be made liable to perform the rent obligation separately in favour of a new owner or transferee. The requirement reflects the principle stated in De Nicols v. Saunders that a person who performs an obligation without notice of a third party’s rights is treated as having discharged it. The Court also relied on Raja Simhadri v. PrattiPatti Ramayya concerning notice before a tenant must split rent payments. Notice affects the tenant’s payment liability, not the time when title passes.

predicates.tenancy_property_severance_case: The case concerns a tenant’s obligations after leased property or the lessor’s interest is severed or transferred.
predicates.tenant_lacks_notice_of_new_owner: The tenant has not received reasonable notice and has no knowledge that another person has become entitled to the relevant rent.
predicates.separate_rent_payment_is_claimed: The new owner seeks to require the tenant to pay rent separately to that owner.

issues.definition: A tenant who has no notice or knowledge of a new owner is not yet liable to pay that owner separately, even though title may already have passed.

issues.legal_issue: When a tenant acquires ownership of a severed portion of the leased property, the tenancy merges into ownership for that portion, leaving the tenant liable as a tenant only for the portion not acquired.
material_facts: During the appeal, the tenant purchased the remaining portion of the shop that had fallen to another family member and had later been gifted to that family member’s wife.
The tenant did not dispute the sale transaction.
The landlord’s eviction suit concerned the portion that had fallen to the landlord, not the portion the tenant purchased.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s interest as tenant merged into his ownership of the purchased portion, so he remained a tenant only in respect of the disputed portion; the landlord’s eviction suit for that portion was maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: When a tenant acquires ownership of part of the leased property, the tenant’s lesser interest as tenant merges into the acquired ownership interest for that part. The lease relationship continues only for any part that the tenant still occupies as a tenant. The Court applied this principle to the undisputed purchase and concluded that the eviction claim concerned a portion in which the tenant had not acquired ownership.

predicates.tenancy_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant from leased property.
predicates.tenant_acquired_ownership_of_severed_por: The tenant acquired ownership of a distinct portion of the leased property.
predicates.eviction_claim_concerns_other_portion: The eviction claim concerns a portion of the leased property that the tenant did not acquire.

issues.definition: If a tenant acquires one distinct portion of leased property and an eviction claim concerns another portion, the tenant owns the acquired portion and remains a tenant of the other portion.
